name: Tartessos
info: Tartessos was a civilisation of the southern Iberian Peninsula, from the late Bronze Age to the 5th century BC, rich in metals, trading with Phoenicians and Greeks, and writing in the Southwest script.

facts.homeland: Western Andalusia around the lower Guadalquivir (the ancient Baetis), Extremadura and southern Portugal; key sites Huelva, the Treasure of El Carambolo at Camas near Seville, La Joya, Medellín, Cástulo, Cancho Roano and Turuñuelo at Guareña
facts.period: Pattern-burnished and "Carambolo" wares from the 9th to the 6th centuries BC; an Early Orientalizing phase from c. 750 BC; an orientalizing phase c. 750–550 BC; most sites abandoned in the 5th century BC, after which the Classic Iberian culture took its place
facts.known: wealth in tin, silver, gold and copper; trade with the Phoenicians of Gadir and with Greek Phocaeans; the Southwest script; King Arganthonios; the gold Treasure of El Carambolo; the earliest mosaic recorded in Western Europe, at Cástulo
facts.sources: Greek and Roman writers including Herodotus, Ephorus, Aristotle, Strabo, Pausanias, Pliny the Elder and Appian; Adolf Schulten's work published in 1922; excavations at El Carambolo from 1958, at Huelva and at Turuñuelo from 2015; carbon-14 dating by the University of Groningen; about 97 inscriptions in the Southwest script

t: Tartessos was the first entity in south-western Iberia recognised as a kingdom, and Herodotus names its king Arganthonios as the host of the first Greeks to reach Iberia.
Its wealth lay in metals: by the Late Bronze Age silver extraction in Huelva Province had reached industrial proportions.
Scholars describe it as a hybrid archaeological culture, formed around the 9th century BC through contact between Phoenician settlers and local people.
dyk: Excavations on two adjoining lots in the centre of Huelva, together 2,150 square metres, yielded some 90,000 fragments of local, Phoenician and Greek pottery dated from the 10th to the early 8th centuries BC.
ev: Huelva becomes a manufacturing and trading harbour receiving goods from distant places
Phoenicians settle in Iberia and build their own harbour at Gadir
The Early Orientalizing phase begins, with the first imports from the eastern Mediterranean
The oldest known indigenous texts of Iberia are written in Tartessian in the Southwest script
A pebble mosaic is laid at Cástulo, the earliest recorded in Western Europe

sections.origins:
Tartessos, as archaeology defines it, was a civilisation settled in the southern Iberian Peninsula from about the late Bronze Age until the 5th century BC. In this region the Tartessian culture was born around the 9th century BC through hybridisation between Phoenician settlers and the local inhabitants, and scholars call it a hybrid archaeological culture. Mining and smelting were older than the arrival of Phoenicians and Greeks, which began in the 8th century BC.

In written records Tartessos appears as a semi-mythical harbour city and its surrounding culture on the south coast of Iberia, at the mouth of the Guadalquivir. It is named in Greek and Near Eastern sources from the first millennium BC; Herodotus placed it beyond the Pillars of Hercules. Aristotle and others called Tartessos a river, and Pausanias described a river with two mouths and a city of the same name between them, which the later Baetis, now the Guadalquivir, seems to fit. Adolf Schulten thought the city might lie buried in the wetlands near the river's mouth, now the Doñana National Park. Tartessian was an extinct pre-Roman language, unclassified for lack of data.
sections.society:
Tartessos was the first entity in south-western Iberia recognised as a kingdom, and Herodotus tells of a king, Arganthonios. Yet its Late Bronze Age sites were not particularly complex, and one mainstream view is that a domestic mode of production predominated. Earlier scholars treated the Tartessians as a less developed people taking up better eastern ways; later ones have looked instead at how local institutions grew.

New finds at Huelva are revising those views. The remains there point to a substantial industrial and commercial emporion that lasted several centuries, and the protohistoric town is estimated at some 20 hectares, large for Iberia in that period. Carbon-14 dates from the University of Groningen and pottery give a sequence of crafts from the 10th century BC: melting pots, casting nozzles, weights, worked wood, ship parts, ivory from the only workshop of its time proven in the west, gold and silver. Houses changed in the 7th and 6th centuries BC from scattered round or oval huts to rectangular houses with dry-stone foundations and plastered wattle-and-daub walls, in planned settlements rebuilt on the same sites.
sections.beliefs:
There is very little evidence for Tartessian religion. It is assumed that, like other Mediterranean peoples, the Tartessians were polytheists, and it is believed that through Phoenician influence they worshipped the goddess Astarte or Potnia and the male god Baal or Melkart. Sanctuaries modelled on Phoenician architecture have been found at Cástulo, near Linares in Jaén, and near Carmona, and images of Phoenician gods have come to light in Cádiz, Huelva and Seville.

At Turuñuelo in Guareña, excavated since 2015 and declared a national heritage site in May 2022, two ornate stone busts were found in 2023. With their jewellery and hairstyles they are thought to be the first known faces of Tartessian goddesses, and they are somewhat similar to the Lady of Elche. Fragments of at least three other busts were also recovered, one of them thought to be a warrior because part of his helmet survives. Burial is known mainly from later sites: no necropolis from before the colonists has been identified, but Medellín on the Guadiana and La Joya at Huelva held rich cemeteries, the latter with hundreds of artefacts.
sections.arts:
Tartessian craft is known through its pottery and metalwork. Distinctive are the fully evolved pattern-burnished wares of the Late Bronze Age and the geometrically banded "Carambolo" wares of the 9th to 6th centuries BC, and later grey ware turned on the fast wheel, thought to imitate imported Phoenician red-slip pottery. The Late Orientalizing phase saw the finest bronze casting and goldsmith work. Characteristic bronzes include pear-shaped jugs, often found in burials with shallow dish-shaped braziers with loop handles, incense burners with floral motifs, fibulas of elbowed and double-spring types, and belt buckles.

In September 1958 the rich gold Treasure of El Carambolo was discovered at Camas, three kilometres west of Seville. At Cástulo a mosaic of river pebbles from the end of the 6th century BC is the earliest mosaic recorded in Western Europe. Tartessos also had writing: the Southwest script, a semi-syllabic system, survives in some 97 inscriptions in an unknown language, the oldest indigenous texts of Iberia, dated to the 7th and 6th centuries BC and found in south-western Spain and southern Portugal.
sections.exchange:
The Tartessians were rich in metals. Alluvial tin was panned in their streams from an early date, and tin, needed for bronze and comparatively rare, was a lucrative trade. In the 4th century BC the historian Ephorus described "a very prosperous market called Tartessos, with much tin carried by river, as well as gold and copper from Celtic lands". The spread of a silver standard in Assyria and the invention of coinage in the 7th century BC raised the demand for silver, and trade, once chiefly in elite goods, took on a broader economic role. Pre-Roman silver slag is found in the Tartessian cities of Huelva Province, and at Riotinto Cypriot and Phoenician metalworkers left 15 million tons of residues.

The Tartessians became important trading partners of the Phoenicians, who built their own harbour at Gadir, present-day Cádiz. Herodotus wrote that Arganthonios welcomed Phocaean Greeks, and Pausanias that the Sicyonian tyrant Myron built a treasury of Tartessian bronze. Huelva holds the largest store of imported elite goods, among them fine Greek painted pottery of the first half of the 6th century BC. These contacts sparked an orientalizing phase in Tartessian culture, c. 750–550 BC.
sections.legacy:
Most Tartessian sites were abandoned in the 5th century BC, for reasons that remain unexplained, and the Classic Iberian culture took the place of the Tartessian. Roman authors mostly repeated the Greek sources, and by around the end of the first millennium BC the name had fallen out of use; the city may have been lost to flooding. Pliny the Elder wrongly identified it with Carteia, and Appian thought Carpia had once been called Tartessos.

The modern search began with Adolf Schulten's discoveries, published in 1922, which moved the study from philologists to archaeologists. J. M. Luzón was the first to identify Tartessos with Huelva, and many archaeologists now link the "lost" city with it. Biblical archaeologists have often identified Tartessos with Tarshish, a place in the Hebrew Bible associated with mineral wealth, while others connect Tarshish with Tarsus in Anatolia or more distant places. Schulten also claimed Tartessos as the source of the legend of Atlantis, and in 2011 Richard Freund announced evidence for it in Doñana; Spanish scientists said he was sensationalising their work and called his claims fanciful.

summary: Tartessos was a culture of southern Iberia from the late Bronze Age to the 5th century BC, grown rich on tin, silver and gold and shaped by trade with Phoenician and Greek merchants. Remembered by Greek writers as a half-legendary city and kingdom, it is now traced through sites such as Huelva and El Carambolo and through inscriptions in the undeciphered Southwest script.
references: Jaime Alvar & José María Blázquez, eds., Los enigmas de Tartessos (Catedra, 1993)
José María Blázquez, Tartessos y los orígenes de la colonización fenicia en Occidente, 2nd edn. (University of Salamanca, 1975)
Fernando González de Canales Cerisola, Jorge Llompart Gómez & Leonardo Serrano Pichardo, El emporio fenicio precolonial de Huelva, ca. 900-770 a.C. (Biblioteca Nueva, 2004)
Sebastián Celestino Pérez & Carolina López-Ruiz, Tartessos and the Phoenicians in Iberia (Oxford University Press, 2016)
notes: The article says the Turuñuelo busts are similar to the Lady of Elche, 'dated between the 5th and 4th centuries BC, considerably earlier' — the logic is confused; I kept only the similarity.
The article's 'silver extraction reached industrial proportions by the Late Bronze Age' sits oddly with the orientalizing chronology; kept as stated.
The 1923 Phoenician necropolis find was left out (unclear location).
End -500 stands for 'the 5th century BC'; start -900 for 'around the 9th century BC' (the article also gives Huelva finds from the 10th century).
The Huelva-Tarshish identification is attributed to 'some scholars' in the article; kept hedged.
